turns.content:
I'm in a Saturday morning ceramics class. There's a guy Julian who always chats with me near the glaze table. Every time, without fail, he pulls out a fresh pack of spearmint gum, takes a piece, then offers me one. I usually accept out of politeness.

It's been three weeks now. I'm starting to wonder — is he hinting my coffee breath is noticeable, or does he just always chew gum while talking?

I'm thinking about asking him next time, something light like: "Be honest, does my morning espresso carry across the room, or are you just generous with mints?"

Would that come off as insecure or awkward? Or is it fine to just keep chewing the gum and drop it.

Short version: this is almost certainly not about your breath. Here's the tell — he takes a piece *himself first*, every time. Someone hinting about your coffee breath would offer you one and skip their own, or pull it out only after you've been talking a while. This is a guy with a gum habit and basic manners. You don't unwrap a pack in front of someone and not offer. That's just the social contract of gum.

Also worth noting: he keeps finding you at the glaze table three weeks running. If your breath were the problem, he'd have quietly relocated to the wheel side of the room.

On your line: it's not insecure, exactly, but it does put him in a spot where the only polite answer is "no, of course not," so you won't actually learn anything, and it's a little confessional for someone you're still getting to know. If you want to poke at it, aim the joke at *him*, not yourself:

- "Okay, three weeks of spearmint. Is this a ritual or a sponsorship deal?"
- Or just bring your own pack next Saturday and offer him one before he can reach for his. That flips the whole thing into a bit, and it's a lot more flirty than asking about your breath.

Or the easiest option: keep taking the gum, say thanks, and enjoy that the guy at the glaze table wants an excuse to stand next to you for a few extra minutes. That's the most likely reading here.

- The pack flipping idea has some appeal. If I brought my own gum and offered it first, it would test whether he offers anyway or just takes mine.

- The sponsorship line is good too. Hits the habit without making it about me at all.

- You are probably right that asking about my breath puts him in an awkward spot. I would rather avoid that.

- One thing I keep noticing though: he does not offer gum to our instructor Frank or to the woman who works the front desk. Just me. That is what keeps me circling back to the breath theory.

- Is it worth testing with my own pack, or am I overcomplicating a guy who just likes spearmint and chatting?

The Frank/front-desk thing is actually the strongest evidence *against* the breath theory, not for it.

Think about who you offer gum to. Not your instructor while he's teaching. Not the person working the desk when you're checking in. You offer it to the person you're standing around shooting the breeze with — and at that class, that's you. He's not withholding gum from Frank; he's just not hanging out with Frank. The "only me" isn't a breath signal, it's a who-am-I-actually-talking-to signal. You're the conversation, so you're the gum recipient.

Also, if someone's trying to hint about breath, they do it once, quietly, maybe twice. They don't build a three-week ritual with a fresh pack each time. That's a guy who's found a comfortable little opener — pull out gum, offer, chat — and he's repeating it because it works. It's a prop, not a message.

On the test: bring the pack. It's zero-cost and kind of delightful either way. But be clear-eyed that it won't actually settle the breath question — if he takes yours and skips his own, that's just manners; if he still produces his spearmint, he's a creature of habit. Neither outcome tells you anything about your espresso. What it *will* tell you is how he reacts to you doing a bit with him. If he grins and plays along ("oh, so it's like that now"), you've got your real answer, and it has nothing to do with mint.

So: not overcomplicating in a bad way, just aiming the microscope at the wrong thing. He's not reacting to your breath. He's reacting to you.

- You make a good point about context. He is not offering to Frank because Frank is busy teaching, not because Frank's breath is fine.

- The prop theory clicks. He probably just found a routine that starts the conversation without awkwardness.

- I think I will bring my own pack next Saturday. If he grins and plays along, that settles it.

- If he still pulls out his own spearmint anyway, what do I do then?

Then you've got a bit, and you lean into it.

Him pulling out his own pack after you've already offered yours isn't a rejection — it's just a habit running on autopilot, and habits are easy to tease. Something like: "Wait, you're not even going to try mine? Is this brand loyalty or are you just not ready to give up control of the gum situation?" That's still aimed at him, still light, and it invites him to be funny back. If he laughs and takes yours anyway, or defends his spearmint like it's a sports team, great — you're now two people with a running joke, which is worth about ten weeks of small talk at the glaze table.

If he takes his own and doesn't react to yours at all, that's still not a breath thing. That's just a guy who's a little on rails and didn't clock the move, which is useful information too — it tells you he's less flirty-playful and more creature-of-routine, and you can adjust your read accordingly.

Either way, the pack has done its job. You've stopped decoding him and started actually interacting with him, and that's the whole point. Bring the gum, have fun with it, and report back — I want to know if he's a spearmint loyalist.

- That is a solid fallback. If he pulls out his own anyway, I will just say something about brand loyalty and see if he bites.

- I think I have enough to go on now. Pack of gum in my bag Saturday morning.

Perfect plan. Gum in the bag, brand-loyalty line in the back pocket, and a glaze table to defend.

One tiny thing: pick something *not* spearmint. Cinnamon, peppermint, whatever. If you show up with the identical pack, it reads as copying; if you bring a rival flavor, it reads as a challenge, and challenges are where the fun is.

Good luck Saturday. Whatever happens, you've already solved the actual mystery — the gum was never about your coffee.
Good advice on the rival flavor. Peppermint it is. I will report back Saturday afternoon.

Peppermint vs. spearmint — the great glaze table mint war of 2026. Go get 'em.

Enjoy the class Saturday, and I'll be curious to hear whether he defends his brand or defects. Either way, you've got a story.
